profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a city government innovation office to organize a three-week effort for redesigning the small-business permit intake process. The context is a cross-department initiative involving Planning, Fire, Licensing, and IT, where the team wants to use two shared artifacts—a proto-service blueprint and a project plan—as boundary objects to align operational knowledge and secure momentum before a budget review. The agenda is to decide what artifacts will be produced, who needs to be involved, how the intake process will be represented, how review will happen, and the timeline for preparing a cross-functional workshop. The expected outcome is an apparently clear division of responsibilities and a schedule for producing a 'first draft,' running a workshop, and obtaining 'validation' before the budget packet deadline.

members.name: Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Service blueprinting, facilitation, cross-functional discovery, artifact-based alignment
members.background: Lena works for a civic-tech consultancy supporting public-sector service redesigns and has led multiple projects where rough visual artifacts were used to surface hidden process differences between agencies.
members.private_state: She wants the workshop artifacts to stay lightweight and exploratory so frontline contradictions emerge early, and she is worried that if the materials become too polished too soon, people will treat them as settled decisions instead of conversation tools.
hidden_assumptions: A 'first draft' of a blueprint is intentionally rough and only needs to be good enough to prompt discussion in a workshop.
The 'right stakeholders' for mapping a service include frontline clerks, permit coordinators, and accessibility staff, not just department managers.
When people say 'intake flow,' they usually mean the real current end-to-end path applicants experience today, including offline handoffs and workarounds.
A process is 'validated' once key contradictions have been surfaced and participants in two offices can work through the artifact without major confusion.

members.name: Daniel Cho
members.expertise: Interdepartmental permitting operations, executive coordination, compliance documentation, internal review processes
members.background: Daniel manages permit intake coordination across several city departments and regularly translates operational changes into materials that directors use for budget and governance decisions.
members.private_state: He wants artifacts that can move quickly into executive circulation with minimal rework, and he is concerned about avoiding informal process changes that have not been documented through established departmental channels.
hidden_assumptions: A 'first draft' is preliminary in content but polished enough to circulate to directors and attach to a budget pre-read.
The 'right stakeholders' are the officially designated process owners for each department; frontline staff can be consulted later if needed.
The 'intake flow' refers to the standardized hybrid intake model discussed in the March steering meeting, even if field practice has not fully caught up.
A process is 'validated' only after the responsible offices review the artifact through the normal approval template and no material objections remain.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to produce a 'first draft' of the blueprint by next Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a low-fidelity working artifact with sticky-note-level detail, suitable for eliciting disagreement in the workshop.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a clean, presentation-ready version that directors could immediately review as part of the budget preparation process.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both routinely use 'first draft' to mean something provisional, so the phrase feels fully sufficient; the hidden difference is about social function and polish level, not the visible task itself.

misalignment_points.topic: Who is included as the 'right stakeholders'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to get the 'right stakeholders' into the workshop and review cycle.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes frontline intake clerks, a call-center representative, and the accessibility coordinator because they carry tacit knowledge about real workarounds.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes only departmental process owners and unit heads because those are the people who can formally represent their offices.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In cross-functional planning, 'stakeholders' is a normal umbrella term and both assume the other shares the obvious participant boundary for a workshop of this type.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss mapping 'the intake flow' before the workshop.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the currently lived intake path applicants experience, including emailed PDFs, walk-in clarifications, and manual routing between counters.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the standardized hybrid intake flow from the March steering meeting, which is the official process model departments are supposed to be using.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe there is one obvious intake flow everyone has in mind; because the current and officially standardized versions share most labels and actors, the reference drift is easy to miss.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to have the process 'validated'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the blueprint should be 'validated with two offices' before finalizing the project plan.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means two offices participate in a walkthrough, can follow the artifact, and surface no major contradictions requiring a structural remap.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the two offices complete the normal review template, provide written comments, and effectively sign off that the representation is acceptable for formal use.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Validation sounds like a routine quality gate and neither person expects that the other is using a materially different threshold for evidence, since both versions plausibly happen after a workshop.

turns.inner_thought: Three weeks is tight, so the artifacts need to do discovery work, not pretend we're already aligned. If I can get a proto-blueprint in front of people early, the frontline contradictions between Planning, Fire, Licensing, and IT will show up fast. The project plan can then reflect what we actually learn instead of locking in assumptions from management summaries.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. What I'd like us to leave with today is a workable approach for the three-week sprint: a proto-service blueprint and a project plan that help Planning, Fire, Licensing, and IT get on the same page before the budget review.

turns.inner_thought: That's the right framing. If we are going to get directors comfortable before budget conversations, we need named owners, dates, and materials that can travel upward without being rebuilt. I need enough structure coming out of this meeting that I can start lining up internal review expectations immediately.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. It would help a lot if we can leave with owners, dates, and something concrete that I can circulate internally so people know what's coming.

turns.inner_thought: I want a rough first draft by next Thursday—boxes, arrows, pain points, exceptions, maybe a few assumptions called out. Just enough for people to react to in the workshop rather than staring at a blank wall. If it's too polished, they'll stop correcting it and start defending it.
turns.utterance: Given the timeline, I'd suggest we have a first draft of the blueprint ready by next Thursday, so the workshop can react to something visible instead of starting from a blank agenda.

turns.inner_thought: A first draft by next Thursday is perfect if it's clean enough to put in front of directors as a preliminary artifact. That gives me time to socialize it upward and get the right stakeholders blocked for the workshop without looking like we're still in note-scrap mode.
turns.utterance: I agree. A first draft by next Thursday would be ideal, because then I can start sharing it upward and make sure the right stakeholders are blocked for the workshop.

turns.inner_thought: I'll start from the lived intake path applicants actually hit today—the online form, emailed attachments, walk-ins who get redirected, manual routing, the clarifications that happen off to the side. The exception paths are where the truth usually is, and I want that in the intake flow before the workshop.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll start by mapping the intake flow first, including the exception paths, so the workshop begins from a shared picture of how requests move across desks and channels.

turns.inner_thought: That should be fairly contained because the intake flow was already settled in March through the steering discussion. What matters now is making sure the official process owners are in the room—Planning intake, Fire review, Licensing administration, and IT systems—so no one later says the workshop got ahead of governance.
turns.utterance: That should help. The intake flow was already aligned in March, so this ought to be a good base to work from. On the workshop side, I can reach out to the unit heads in Planning, Fire, Licensing, and IT as the key stakeholders.

turns.inner_thought: One workshop should be enough to surface the big disconnects if the artifact is loose enough. After that, if two offices can walk through it without major confusion and we aren't discovering structural contradictions, I'll treat it as validated and fold what we learned into the project plan.
turns.utterance: My thought is that we run one workshop, then validate the blueprint with two offices before I fold the feedback into the project plan.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, once two offices validate it through the normal review process, I'll have something I can treat as confirmed for formal use. At that point I can send around the usual review template and start turning the process description into material that directors can rely on.
turns.utterance: That works for me. Once two offices validate it, I can treat the process description as confirmed and send around the usual review template.

turns.inner_thought: I'll own the rough blueprint build. But I need more than department leads in the room if we want the real service picture: at least one intake clerk and the accessibility coordinator, ideally someone who sees the workarounds every day. Those are part of the right stakeholders, not optional add-ons.
turns.utterance: Okay, then I'll take the draft blueprint. If you can help line up participants, I'd like to make sure we have the right stakeholders in the workshop and review cycle, including an intake clerk and the accessibility coordinator along with the department leads.

turns.inner_thought: I'll send her the March deck so she has the official intake flow as the source, reserve time with the department owners, and watch for the first draft Thursday. If that draft is presentable, I can fold it into Friday's packet preparation without losing momentum.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll send you the March intake deck, reserve time with the department owners, and look for the first draft on Thursday so we stay on track for Friday's packet deadline.
